questions.prompt: The source list changes after the query is defined but before it is iterated. What does this print?
questions.explanation: `Where` is deferred: the query runs only during the `foreach`, after `5` was added, so the new element is included.

questions.prompt: This time the query ends with `ToList()`. What does it print?
questions.explanation: `ToList()` executed the query immediately and stored the results, so adding `5` to the source afterwards doesn't affect `result`.

questions.prompt: `var query = numbers.Where(n => n > 2);` has been defined. Which of these makes it execute?
options: Assigning it to another variable: `var q2 = query;`
Nothing; it already ran when it was defined
questions.explanation: A deferred query runs only when you iterate it or call a method that forces execution, such as materialization methods (`ToList()`, `ToArray()`) or aggregation methods (`Count()`, `Sum()`, `First()`, `Any()`).

questions.prompt: According to the comparison table, what is a cost of immediate execution compared with deferred execution?
options: It always reflects the latest data, so results can change unexpectedly
It re-runs the query every time you loop over the result
It uses more memory, because it stores all the results
It cannot be used with `Count()` or `Sum()`
questions.explanation: Immediate execution stores all results (higher memory) and uses a snapshot taken at query time, while deferred execution streams results and reflects the latest data.

options: `ToLookup()` executes immediately and returns a read-only `ILookup` you can reuse
`ToLookup()` allows only one value per key
questions.explanation: `ToLookup()` groups like `GroupBy()`, but it executes immediately and returns an immutable one-to-many `ILookup<TKey, TElement>` that is already evaluated and can be reused efficiently.
